         Rational degree is polynomially related to degree
                         Matt Kovacs-Deak∗           Daochen Wang†              Rain Zimin Yang‡

                                                        Abstract
                                              4
         We prove that deg(f ) ≤ 2 rdeg(f ) for every Boolean function f , where deg(f ) is the degree of
         f and rdeg(f ) is the rational degree of f . This resolves the second of the three open problems
         stated by Nisan and Szegedy, and attributed to Fortnow, in 1994 [NS94].


1       Introduction
The degree deg(f ) of a Boolean function f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1} is the minimum value of deg(r) such
that r is a real polynomial and f = r on {0, 1}n . The rational degree rdeg(f ) of f is the minimum
value of max(deg(p), deg(q)) such that p, q are real polynomials and f = p/q on {0, 1}n . Clearly,
rdeg(f ) ≤ deg(f ) as can be seen by taking the denominator q to be 1. On the other hand, it is
unclear whether rdeg(f ) could be much smaller than degree.
    Degree is polynomially related to almost all Boolean complexity measures. Rational degree
characterizes the exact postselected quantum query complexity [MdW15]. Whether rational degree
is polynomially related to degree has remained an open problem since it was first stated by Nisan
and Szegedy, and attributed to Fortnow, over three decades ago [NS94].
    Since then, the problem has been reiterated in works such as [dW00; dW01; dW03; MdW15;
Cade20; ABK+21; IJK+25]. Rational degree can also be motivated from a variety of perspectives
beyond quantum postselection:
1. The analogous randomized query measure, exact postselected randomized query complexity,
   equals the certificate complexity [Cade20, Theorem 16]. Therefore, rational degree can be viewed
   as a natural quantum notion of certificate complexity. (Note that rational degree is distinct from
   Aaronson’s definition of quantum certificate complexity [Aar08].)
2. We have deg± (f ) ≤ 2 rdeg(f ) by squaring and shifting p, where deg± (f ) is the sign degree (or
   threshold degree) of f , that is, the minimum degree of a real polynomial that agrees in sign
   with (−1)f (x) for all x ∈ {0, 1}n . Therefore, deg± (f )/2 ≤ rdeg(f ) ≤ deg(f ). Sign degree and
   degree are well-studied complexity measures [Saks20; NS94; O’D14]. As rational degree inherits
   structural properties of both, it helps us better understand their relationship.
3. It is not hard to see that rdeg(f ) = max(ndeg(f ), ndeg(¬f )), where ¬ denotes negation and
   ndeg(f ) is the minimum degree of a real polynomial s such that, for all x ∈ {0, 1}n , s(x) = 0
   if and only if f (x) = 0. (This is Fact 3, for which we give a proof for completeness.) In
   combinatorics, the Alon-Füredi theorem [AF93] is equivalent to ndeg(ANDn ) = n, and the key
   lemma of [ABCO88] essentially shows ndeg(PARITYn ) ≥ n/2. At a deeper level, the relation
   between rational degree and degree governs the effectiveness of a natural Nullstellensatz for the
   hypercube, in the sense of [Bro87; Kol88; Alon99; Jel05]. We give more details in Section 4.1.
4. In complexity theory, ndeg(f ) equals the degree of the set f −1 (0) as defined by Smolensky [Smo93],
   and equals the one-sided 0-approximate degree of f , up to a factor of 2, as defined by Sherstov
   [She18]. Polynomially relating rational degree to degree also implies P = (C= P ∩ co-C= P) with
   respect to generic oracles [FFKL03]. This originally motivated Fortnow to pose his open problem
   [For26], which he has described as one of his “favorite and most frustrating” [For03].

    In this work, we resolve the open problem by proving deg(f ) ≤ 2 rdeg(f )4 for every Boolean
function f . In fact, we prove the stronger result that deg(f ) ≤ O(deg± (f )2 rdeg(f )2 ). We end by
discussing a variety of implications and open problems.

2.1        Boolean functions
A Boolean function is a function of the form f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1}, where n is a positive integer. The
degree of f is defined using the following well-known fact, see, e.g., [BdW02, Lemma 1].

Fact 1 (Multilinear representation). For every f : {0, 1}n → R, there exists a unique multilinear
p ∈ R[X1 , . . . , Xn ] such that p(x) = f (x) for all x ∈ {0, 1}n .

Definition 1 (Degree). The degree of f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1}, denoted deg(f ), is defined to be the
degree of the unique multilinear p ∈ R[X1 , . . . , Xn ] such that p(x) = f (x) for all x ∈ {0, 1}n .

        We now give the definitions of rational degree, sign degree and nondeterministic degree.

Definition 2 (Rational degree). We say that p/q ∈ R(X1 , . . . , Xn ), where p, q are multilinear, is a
rational representation of f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1} if for all x ∈ {0, 1}n , q(x) ̸= 0 and p(x)/q(x) = f (x).
The rational degree of f , denoted rdeg(f ), is the minimum value of max(deg(p), deg(q)) over all
rational representations of f .

Definition 3 (Sign degree). We say that p ∈ R[X1 , . . . , Xn ], where p is multilinear, is a sign
representation of f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1} if p(x) ̸= 0 for all x ∈ {0, 1}n , and p(x) < 0 if and only if
f (x) = 1. The sign degree of f , denoted deg± (f ), is the minimum value of deg(p) over all sign
representations of f .

Definition 4 (Nondeterministic degree). We say that p ∈ R[X1 , . . . , Xn ], where p is multilinear, is
a nondeterministic representation of f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1} if for all x ∈ {0, 1}n , p(x) ̸= 0 if and only if
f (x) = 1. The nondeterministic degree of f , denoted ndeg(f ), is the minimum value of deg(p) over
all nondeterministic representations of f .

        We record the following fact relating rational degree to sign degree mentioned in the introduction.

Fact 2. For every Boolean function f , deg± (f )/2 ≤ rdeg(f ).1

   Our proof will use the following characterization of rational degree in terms of nondeterministic
degrees. The result is folklore and we give a proof for completeness.

Fact 3. For every Boolean function f , rdeg(f ) = max(ndeg(f ), ndeg(¬f )).

Proof. Let p/q be a rational representation of f with max(deg(p), deg(q)) = rdeg(f ). Then, p and
q − p are nondeterministic representations of f and ¬f respectively. Thus,

max(ndeg(f ), ndeg(¬f )) ≤ max(deg(p), deg(q − p)) ≤ max(deg(p), max(deg(p), deg(q))) = rdeg(f ).

   Conversely, let p and q be nondeterministic representations of f and ¬f respectively, with
deg(p) = ndeg(f ) and deg(q) = ndeg(¬f ). Then p/(p + q) is a rational representation of f . Thus,

rdeg(f ) ≤ max(deg(p), deg(p + q)) ≤ max(deg(p), max(deg(p), deg(q))) = max(ndeg(f ), ndeg(¬f )).

   Taken together, we obtain rdeg(f ) = max(ndeg(f ), ndeg(¬f )), as required.

   We also record the fact that rational degree exactly equals the ϵ-approximate postselected
quantum query complexity PostQϵ with ϵ = 0 as defined in [MdW15]. We will not use this fact later
but it serves to underscore the tight connection between rational degree and quantum complexity, a
connection first observed by Aaronson [Aar05].

   Our proof will relate rational degree to degree via the following three complexity measures.

Definition 5 (Block sensitivity). Let f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1}. Let x ∈ {0, 1}n . We say that a subset
B ⊆ [n] is a sensitive block of f at x if f (x) ̸= f (xB ), where xB denotes x with all bits in B flipped.
The block sensitivity of f at x, denoted bsx (f ), is the maximum number of disjoint sensitive blocks
of f at x.

Definition 6 (Hitting set). For a multilinear polynomial p := S⊆[n] cS · i∈S Xi ∈ R[X1 , . . . , Xn ],
its set of maxonomials is the set M(p) := {M ⊆ [n] : |M | = deg(p), cM ̸= 0}. We say that H ⊆ [n]
is a hitting set of p if H ∩ M is nonempty for all M ∈ M(p).

Definition 7 (Decision tree complexity). The decision tree complexity of f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1},
denoted D(f ), is the minimum depth of a decision tree that, for all x ∈ {0, 1}n , queries bits of x to
exactly compute f (x) at a leaf.

Theorem 3 ([NS94, Lemma 2.6]). Let p ∈ R[X1 , . . . , Xn ] be a nonzero multilinear polynomial.

assignment. Therefore, Pr[p(x) ̸= 0] ≥ 2−n · 2n−deg(p) = 2− deg(p) .

4      Implications and open problems
4.1    Effective Hypercube Nullstellensatz
The main result of this work can be framed as an effective Hypercube Nullstellensatz.

Theorem 5 (Effective Hypercube Nullstellensatz). Let g1 , g2 ∈ R[X1 , . . . , Xn ]. Suppose g1 and g2
do not share any common zeros on the hypercube {0, 1}n . Further suppose g1 (x) · g2 (x) = 0 for all
x ∈ {0, 1}n . Then there exist h1 , h2 ∈ R[X1 , . . . , Xn ] such that

                            h1 (x)g1 (x) + h2 (x)g2 (x) = 1    for all x ∈ {0, 1}n ,                         (19)

and
                            max(deg(h1 g1 ), deg(h2 g2 )) ≤ 2 deg(g1 )2 deg(g2 )2 ,                          (20)
where the overline denotes multilinearization using the relations X12 = X1 , . . . , Xn2 = Xn .

Proof. Construct polynomials h1 , h2 satisfying Eq. (19) by interpolation. We proceed to bound
max(deg(h1 g1 ), deg(h2 g2 )). Define f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1} by f (x) = 0 if and only if g1 (x) = 0. Then by
the hypotheses of the theorem, g1 , g2 are nondeterministic representations of f and ¬f , respectively.
For every x ∈ {0, 1}n , we have h1 (x)g1 (x) = f (x) and h2 (x)g2 (x) = ¬f (x). Therefore by uniqueness
of multilinear representation, we deduce max(deg(h1 g1 ), deg(h2 g2 )) = max(deg(f ), deg(¬f )), and
the theorem follows from Corollary 4.

to any number of polynomials holds.

4.4       Improving polynomial relations
Since degree is polynomially related to almost all other Boolean complexity measures, Corollary 3
immediately yields polynomial relations between rational degree and those measures too. It would
be interesting to see the extent to which these polynomial relations could be tightened. More
specifically, this work turns all question marks in [IJK+25, Table 1] into the number 4, but can we
obtain matching numbers?
   We conjecture that Corollary 3 is optimal with respect to D versus rdeg.
Conjecture 4. There exists a family of Boolean functions f such that D(f ) ≥ Ω(rdeg(f )4 ).
    The currently best-known separation is quadratic. It can be witnessed by at least two different
functions: the balanced AND-OR tree,9 or the “pointer function” that quadratically separates D
from exact quantum query complexity [ABB+17].
    We note that [dW03, Section 4] conjectured10 D(f ) ≤ O(ndeg(f ) · ndeg(¬f )) for every Boolean
function f . If true, this would falsify Conjecture 4. However, at the time [dW03] was published,
contrived Boolean functions like those constructed in [ABK16; ABB+17] were unknown. More
recently (in 2026), Ronald de Wolf informed us of a weaker conjecture:
                                                ?
                                       QE (f ) ≤ O(ndeg(f ) · ndeg(¬f )),                                        (37)
where QE denotes the exact quantum query complexity of f . If Eq. (37) held, it would be a quantum
counterpart to the classical fact D(f ) ≤ C0 (f ) · C1 (f ), where Cb denotes the b-certificate complexity.
